power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: To estimate the minimum number of participants to be recruited for data collection, the ratio of the number of cases (N) to the number of model parameters that require statistical estimates (q) was considered. In accordance with Kline (2023), a recommended N:q would be 20:1. As the number of model parameters that require statistical estimates with respect to the structural equation model of interest in the present registered report equals q = 45 (see Footnote 1), the number of cases thus equals N = 20*q = 20*45 = 900. By performing structural equation model power analyses using the R package semPower version 2.1.3 (Moshagen & Bader, 2025), considering N = 900 and a = 0.050, the structural equation model of interest in the present registered report would yield a power 1-b = 0.85 (b = 0.15) to detect modelimplied g standardized estimates g = 0.10. Additionally, we conservatively estimated based on prior research using the same participant recruitment method and source (Xiao, Fraser, et al., 2024) that data collected from approximately 20% of participants would be excluded from analysis because, despite being video game players, they did not play any games containing loot boxes and so were not exposed to nor had any opportunities to purchase that specific form of gambling-like products, and in addition, they also did not report purchasing any physical gambling-like products, such as blind boxes and card packs. This exclusion ensured that the sample consisted of participants who were exposed to and had the opportunity to purchase at least one form of digital gambling-like products (e.g., video game loot boxes) and/or had purchased at least one physical gambling-like product. Further, we anticipated that data collected from approximately 10% of participants would be excluded for satisfying other exclusion criteria detailed below. Accordingly, we preregistered terminating data collection upon reaching N = 900*(1/((100-20)/100))*(1/((100-10)/100)) = 1,250.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. All participants were asked to complete the PGSI regardless of their past-year gambling participation status, emulating previous research to maximize usable data (Xiao et al., 2026; cf. Xiao, Newall, et al., 2024).

text.text: Gambling-like products share structural and psychological characteristics with legally regulated traditional gambling but are generally not regulated as gambling.
Virtual gambling-like products include video game loot boxes, whilst physical gambling-like products include blind boxes and card packs.
Stakeholders are concerned about the potential harms of these globally popular products, including overspending and the normalization of gambling amongst children.
We surveyed Mainland Chinese video game players (final N = 913) to investigate whether spending on various gambling-like products is associated with problem gambling severity.
Replicating previous results, we found weak-but practically meaningfulassociations between problem gambling severity and both digital loot box and physical card pack spending.
In contrast, the association between problem gambling and physical blind box spending was very weak and arguably not practically meaningful.
Fundamental differences at the product characteristic-level mean that some gambling-like products, like blind boxes, may be less risky, but further research is warranted.
Thus, a cautious and balanced approach with a focus on product transparency and child protection should be taken when regulating gambling-like products.
Blind box regulation may justifiably be light-touch, whilst loot box and card pack regulations could be stricter and more restrictive, given a greater potential for harm.

Gambling-like products share structural and psychological characteristics with legally regulated traditional gambling (e.g., roulette and slot machines) but are generally not regulated as gambling.

For example, players can (i) spend money to buy "loot boxes" or engage with "gacha" mechanics inside video games to (ii) obtain random virtual rewards, most of which are worth little, but a few rare rewards are highly valuable.

text.text: In summary, previous research suggests that the relationship between problem gambling and physical gambling-like products is weaker than that between problem gambling and virtual gambling-like products (e.g., video game loot boxes).
However, no research on the relationship between blind box purchasing and problem gambling has been conducted, despite an obvious international need due to their recent popularity.
Furthermore, no research on the relationship between card pack purchasing and problem gambling has been conducted in non-English-speaking contexts.

Therefore, in the present study, we extend on previous research (see Xiao et al., 2026) to better understand the relationships between problem gambling and gambling-like products that are not (yet) regulated as gambling (i.e., (i) video game loot boxes, (ii) physical blind boxes, and (iii) physical card packs) in a sample of people living in Mainland China.

text.text: We anticipated that the vast majority of our respondents would be aged 18 or above.
However, the platform did allow under-18 users to join and be recruited as potential panel participants for surveys.
It was technically possible to pay the platform to exclude under-18s from being recruited.
However, the costs associated with doing so were disproportionately high.
Therefore, we asked all participants to confirm that they were aged 18 or above and excluded under-18s.

Upon satisfying any of the exclusion criteria through the initial screening phase, the respondent was informed that they did not satisfy the eligibility criteria, and their survey was thereupon terminated.
Further, we included three interspersed attention checks throughout the survey and excluded the participants who failed two or more of them.
Firstly, participants were asked to correctly answer a simple arithmetic question ("3+5=?").
Secondly, participants were asked whether they had played a non-existent, fictional video game in the past 12 months (i.e., a nonsensical item).
Thirdly, participants were tested using an instructional manipulation check, in which they were asked to select two specific options.

Finally, at the end of the survey, participants were asked whether, in their honest opinion and with no influence on their payment, their data should be used for the researchers' analyses (Meade & Craig, 2012).

In this light, the present results cannot provide evidence that spending on physical gambling-like products is associated with the severity of gambling-related problems differently (i.e., to a lesser or greater extent) than spending on digital gambling-like products is associated with the severity of gambling-related problems.
The current study investigated whether spending on various gambling-like products such as blind boxes, card packs, and loot boxes was associated with the severity of gambling-related problems.

We also aimed to-but could not-provide evidence on whether spending on physical gambling-like products (such as blind boxes and card packs) is associated with the severity of gambling-related problems differently than spending on digital gambling-like products (such as loot boxes) is associated with the severity of gambling-related problems.
To test these, we conducted an online survey of a convenience sample of Mainland Chinese video game players, a demographic we expected to be most likely to engage with gambling-like products.
Our results suggest that engagement with all gambling-like products are positively associated with problem gambling severity.
Specifically, spending money on gambling-like physical blind boxes was positively associated with problem gambling.

However, this relationship is very weak and falls below the conventional smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) for research on media effects, i.e., R² ≥ 1% (Drummond et al., 2020, p. 11; Ferguson, 2009 Ferguson, , pp. 532-533, 2023, p. 3, p. 3) and should therefore be interpreted as practically not meaningful.

text.text: In contrast, spending money on digital loot boxes in video games and on physical card packs were weakly positively associated with problem gambling with effect sizes that are practically meaningful, replicating previous loot box findings in Mainland China (Xiao, Fraser, et al., 2024) and internationally (Garea et al., 2021; González-Cabrera et al., 2023; Palmer et al., 2025; Spicer, Nicklin, et al., 2022; Zendle & Cairns, 2018) and a previous anglophone country physical card pack study (Xiao et al., 2026).

text.text: Notably, when we controlled for age, gender identity, and monthly disposable income as preregistered, all effects became slightly stronger.

Specifically, the effect size for the relationship between blind box spending and problem gambling crossed the threshold for the conventional SESOI and therefore could also be interpreted as practically meaningful.

Given these borderline results, further research is needed as our results suggest limited, weak evidence at best that problem gambling severity may be a very small factor that is relevant to blind box engagement, potentially leading to some harm.
This association certainly is not capable on its own to explain any associations previously found between blind box engagement and suicide risk (Duan et al., 2022).

text.text: Our study, being cross-sectional in design, cannot make any causal claims about blind box engagement leading to consumers experiencing gambling harm or blind boxes being "addictive" in a scientific sense.

Nevertheless, the lack of strong evidence for population-level risks does not mean that specific consumers, who may be so-called "outliers" (Petrovskaya & Zendle, 2023, p. 12), do not experience individual-level harm and should be especially studied and duly supported.

text.text: Potential explanations for the association between blind box spending and problem gambling being negligible include that even the more desirable "secret rare" toy from blind boxes (e.g., a Labubu with a 1/72 chance of being obtained) could be easily purchased directly on popular and well-stocked secondary markets in Mainland China, like 闲鱼 [Xianyu] (Goofish.com), at a price equivalent to that of merely two or three blind boxes.

Therefore, in practice, consumers are unlikely to buy many blind boxes when trying to obtain a secret rare toy, since they have a cheaper, nonrandomized, and not gambling-like alternative acquisition method.

In contrast, most video game loot box rewards cannot be transferred between users: players must win them personally (Xiao & Henderson, 2024), forcing them to spend money on the gambling mechanism of opening many loot boxes.

text.text: Similarly, card packs are also fundamentally different from blind boxes: for example, the rarest prizes from physical card packs, while they can be bought on the secondary market, are often very expensive and can cost as much as dozens of card packs (Kim, 2023).

text.text: Another distinction between blind boxes on the one hand and loot boxes and card packs on the other is that many consumers will be satisfied with the blind box opening regardless of its result: they wish merely to obtain a toy and, having already chosen from a series they prefer, any random toy would be acceptable, even if the rarer, specific ones would have been more exciting and desirable (Wei & Yu, 2025, p. 15178).

text.text: In contrast, the vast majority of loot box and card pack openings lead to disappointing results that the consumer can derive very little value from: consumers would desire only to open and obtain specific rare rewards, and most often fail, thus encouraging them to try again by spending more money, rendering these products more similar to traditional gambling.
Thus, "loss chasing" (Zhang & Clark, 2020) would often be present in loot box and card pack engagement, but may be less relevant to blind boxes.

text.text: The nuanced product characteristics of all gambling-like products and consumers' motivations for engaging with them should be further scrutinized and, where appropriate, differentiated.

In light of weak evidence at best linking gambling-like products (particularly, in relation to blind boxes, but also with loot boxes and card packs to a more limited extent) to traditional gambling harms (Sidloski et al., 2022), despite apparent structural and psychological similarities, the appropriate regulatory response should be cautious and balanced whilst the evidence base develops.

text.text: The risks to more vulnerable consumers, including young children and people already experiencing gambling problems, and the unlikelihood of these products causing widespread and substantial harm to adults should both be recognized.
Policies that do not overly restrict-particularly adults' engagementand instead seek to provide more transparency so that consumers can make more informed purchasing decisions are more justifiable.
Stricter loot box and card pack regulations are more justifiable, given a greater potential for harm.

text.text: The lack of relevant regulatory policies in other countries may mean that blind box engagement remains more gambling-like elsewhere, and thus the associations are stronger.

Surveys about blind box engagement and problem gambling should be conducted in other cultural contexts, considering that these products are globally popular and may be affecting different populations in varied ways.
In our study, we distinguished between physical and digital gambling-like products based on the definitions we provided to our participants.
However, these mediumbased boundaries are increasingly blurring.

POP MART's official POP NOW feature allows consumers to purchase physical blind boxes through its online shop, with the unboxing result immediately revealed digitally and the physical product delivered in person only after some time has passed.

Clove is a mobile app through which consumers can purchase digital "loot boxes" containing physical trading card products that could later be delivered, whilst Whatnot is a different app through which content creators sell physical card packs that are then opened live on stream.

When a consumer spends money through such hybrid product offerings, it becomes more difficult to determine whether they have spent on a physical product, a virtual service, or something else entirely with unique risk factors.
Physical blind boxes and card packs and digital loot boxes in video games are internationally popular gambling-like products.
They offer random prizes and thus share structural and psychological characteristics with legally regulated traditional gambling.
However, they are generally not regulated as such at present.
Concerns have been raised about their potential harms, including overspending and underage engagement.
We thus conducted an online survey of adult Mainland Chinese video game players (N = 913).
We replicated previous research findings and found weak but practically meaningful links between problem gambling and both digital loot box and physical card pack spending.
In contrast, we found only a very weak association between problem gambling and blind box spending that was arguably not practically meaningful.

Various product characteristics that differentiate various gambling-like products, such as the rare prizes being alternatively acquirable through direct purchase from the secondary market at a reasonable price, which may have reduced the gambling-like nature and potential riskiness and harm of blind boxes.
Given these fundamental differences, various gambling-like products should be separately studied.
A cautious and balanced approach with a focus on product transparency and child protection should be taken when regulating gambling-like products.
Blind box regulation may justifiably be light-touch, whilst loot box and card pack regulations could be stricter and more restrictive, given a great potential for harm.
